items.q: Is Shopify or Webflow cheaper for an online store?
items.a: It depends on billing terms, but Shopify usually costs less for a straightforward store. As of 26 September 2026, Shopify's Basic plan is $39 a month and includes unlimited products, hosting and a point-of-sale system, with no extra fee when the store uses Shopify Payments. Webflow's cheapest real store plan, Ecommerce Standard, is $42 a month, caps the catalog at 500 items, and always charges a 2% fee on top of whatever Stripe or PayPal already takes. Billed yearly, the two plans land at almost the same price, $29 a month each, which makes the fee the deciding factor rather than the sticker price. A larger catalog that needs Webflow's fee-free Ecommerce Plus tier, at $84 a month, or Advanced, at $235, will generally cost more than the equivalent Shopify plan for the same size of team.

items.q: Does Webflow charge a transaction fee the way Shopify does?
items.a: Yes, but only on its cheapest ecommerce tier. Webflow's Ecommerce Standard plan charges a 2% fee on every sale, on top of whatever Stripe or PayPal already charges, no matter which of those two processors you use. Upgrading to Ecommerce Plus, at $84 a month, removes that fee entirely, as does Ecommerce Advanced at $235. Shopify works the other way around: there is no Shopify fee at all when a store uses Shopify Payments, Shop Pay or PayPal Express Checkout, on any plan including the $39 Basic plan. Shopify only adds a fee, 2% on Basic, 1% on Grow or 0.6% on Advanced, when a store chooses a different payment processor instead. A store committed to Shopify Payments can avoid a platform fee at a lower price than a store on Webflow can.

items.q: Can I sell more than a few hundred products on Webflow?
items.a: Only by moving up Webflow's ecommerce tiers, and each one has its own cap. Ecommerce Standard, at $42 a month, stops at 500 items. Ecommerce Plus, at $84 a month, raises that to 5,000 items and also removes the 2% transaction fee that Standard charges. Ecommerce Advanced, at $235 a month, goes up to 15,000 items. Shopify does not use this kind of ceiling at all: every paid plan, starting with the $39 Basic plan, allows an unlimited product count, so a growing catalog never forces a plan change on Shopify the way it eventually will on Webflow. A store that expects real catalog growth should weigh Webflow's item caps carefully before committing to it as the platform for that growth.

items.q: Is Shopify or Webflow better for a business that is mostly a marketing site with a small store attached?
items.a: Often Webflow, if the content is the bigger job and the store stays small. Webflow's Premium plan, at $39 a month, is built as a CMS plan: 20,000 items across 40 Collections, which is the kind of content depth a blog, resource library or multi-page marketing site actually needs, while Shopify's blog tools exist but were not built for that scale of general content. Selling products on Webflow means picking one of its separate Ecommerce plans instead, starting at $42 a month for Ecommerce Standard, and Webflow's pricing page does not spell out whether that plan carries Premium's same CMS depth alongside the store, so confirm that specific limit with Webflow before assuming the two come bundled together. A business whose real product is its content, with a small catalog on the side, is the case Webflow fits best; a business built around a large or growing catalog is better served by Shopify.

items.q: How much does it cost to add staff on Shopify compared with Webflow?
items.a: On Shopify, often nothing, up to a point. As of 26 September 2026, Basic includes no staff accounts beyond the store owner, but Grow, at $105 a month, includes up to 5, and Advanced, at $399, includes up to 15, all with no separate per-person charge. Webflow bills every added editor as its own line: a Full seat costs $45 a month and a Limited seat costs $19 a month, on top of whatever Site plan and bandwidth the site already needs. A small Shopify team usually pays nothing extra for staff logins until it needs the next plan tier, while the same team on Webflow pays for every seat every month, which adds up faster than either company's plan price alone suggests.

items.q: Why does Webflow's bill grow so much as traffic increases?
items.a: Because Webflow meters bandwidth and Shopify does not. Webflow's Premium plan includes 50 GB of bandwidth a month, and a site that outgrows that buys a bandwidth add-on, in tiers that reach $560 a month for 1 TB. A busy content site with real traffic can end up paying more for bandwidth alone than for the Premium plan itself. Shopify has no equivalent charge on any plan: its higher tiers cost more because of staff-account limits and card-rate improvements, not because of how many people visit the store. Webflow's own pricing page describes bandwidth in a page-view range rather than an exact per-visit figure, so the tier a given site needs is an estimate that heavier pages, video or bot traffic can push higher.

items.q: Can I move my store from Shopify to Webflow, or the other way around, later?
items.a: Plan for a rebuild either way, not a quick migration. A Shopify store only runs on Shopify's own servers, so switching away from it, to Webflow or anywhere else, means recreating the storefront and checkout on the new platform. Webflow gives back more of the raw material: a paid Workspace plan can export a site's HTML and CSS, so the visual design does not have to be rebuilt from scratch. That export leaves out the CMS content, which comes out one Collection at a time, and the cart, checkout and form logic, all of which still need rebuilding on whatever platform comes next. Neither platform makes leaving free or fast, so budget real time for a full switch in either direction, not a weekend project.
